# AI governance has moved from policy debate to control evidence

*As of 2026-10-18. Part 1 of 3 in the Agentic GRC series.*

The important shift is not that autonomous agents are suddenly running critical infrastructure; it is that AI capabilities are being translated into existing control categories that operators already govern. [01-c5]

The clearest evidence comes from the US electricity sector, where recent items connect AI to access control, BES cyber-system evaluation, threat detection logic and computational-load reliability requirements. [01-c1] [01-c2] [01-c3] [01-c5]

That matters because governance becomes enforceable when an abstract technology is mapped to accountable owners, authorized access, monitored communications paths, operational data and evidence that controls are working. [01-c5]

## What changed

Industrial Cyber reported that FERC staff’s 2026 CIP audit lessons highlighted access-control risks from “super intelligence” tools, including chatbots, personal assistants and automated analytical systems, as those tools become embedded in networks supporting critical infrastructure protection assets. [01-c1]

That is a reported fact about how FERC staff framed the issue in audit lessons, not proof that autonomous AI agents are operating critical assets. [01-c1]

The practical point is narrower and more important for governance: AI-like tools in CIP-networked environments become part of access-control and monitoring questions. [01-c1]

Industrial Cyber also reported FERC staff’s view that CIP Reliability Standards neither explicitly allow nor prohibit these tools, but that entities should consider their risks when evaluating BES Cyber Systems and apply appropriate controls. [01-c5]

That is the governance hinge: even without an “AI standard,” AI features can affect how an entity categorizes systems, assesses risk and demonstrates control coverage. [01-c5]

For executives, this turns AI governance from a policy discussion into an evidence problem. [01-c5]

The question is no longer only “Do we have an AI policy?” but “Where do AI tools touch regulated environments, who can use them, what systems can they influence, and what control evidence proves that risk has been assessed?” [01-c1] [01-c5]

## The grid-load issue is becoming a reliability issue

Utility Dive reported that NERC stakeholders approved new reliability standards for AI data centers, crypto mining facilities and other computational loads, describing the vote as an important step toward finalization. [01-c2]

That is a reported fact about the standards process, not a statement that the standards are already fully enforceable in every relevant setting. [01-c2]

Still, it shows AI infrastructure moving from a planning concern toward formal grid-reliability requirements. [01-c2]

The proposed standards are described as requiring transmission operators, balancing authorities and reliability coordinators to have computational-load site data needed to plan, monitor and assess reliable bulk-power operation. [01-c5]

They are also described as establishing communications capabilities with predefined protocols so responsible parties can take prompt action to prevent or mitigate events that adversely affect bulk-power reliability. [01-c5]

This is not “AI safety” in the broad public-policy sense. [01-c5]

It is reliability governance: know the load, model the load, communicate with the load, and define the operational pathways for mitigation. [01-c5]

For critical-infrastructure operators, that framing is familiar. [01-c5]

The new element is that AI data-center demand is becoming large and operationally significant enough to be handled through reliability standards rather than treated only as a commercial interconnection or capacity-planning question. [01-c2] [01-c5]

## Threat models are absorbing AI-assisted activity

Industrial Cyber reported that MITRE ATT&CK v20 added campaigns documenting attacks on more than 30 Minnesota water and wastewater utilities and an AI-assisted breach of Mexican government infrastructure that crossed IT and OT environments and reached a municipal water utility. [01-c3]

That is a reported fact about threat-modeling coverage, not evidence that AI-assisted intrusions are now common across all critical-infrastructure sectors. [01-c3]

The significance is that AI-assisted activity is being represented inside a framework defenders already use to describe adversary behavior. [01-c3]

Industrial Cyber also reported that MITRE expanded enterprise coverage with techniques addressing prompt injection, AI-enabled data exfiltration, AI result poisoning and attacks targeting AI-assisted defenses. [01-c5]

That matters because it converts AI risk into detection logic, analytic assumptions and defensive test cases. [01-c5]

For CISOs and OT security leaders, the useful question is not whether every attacker is now “agentic.” [01-c3] [01-c5]

The useful question is whether existing monitoring, incident response and threat-hunting processes can recognize AI-enabled data movement, manipulation of AI outputs and attacks against AI-assisted defensive tools. [01-c5]

## What to make of the practitioner signal

Dragos, speaking from an OT security practitioner and vendor perspective, says AI in OT offense and defense is no longer only conference hype. [01-c4]

In the cited remarks, Dragos says it avoided making strong AI claims earlier because it did not see authentic field use cases for offense or defense, but that in 2026 it now has a view and considers the issue real. [01-c4]

That should be treated as a source claim, not independent proof of systemic prevalence. [01-c4]

Dragos has commercial incentives in the OT security market, so its assessment is useful as field interpretation but should be corroborated before being treated as sector-wide evidence. [01-c4]

The governance response visible in the other evidence is also more concrete than the broad claim that “AI is real now.” [01-c1] [01-c2] [01-c3] [01-c5]

FERC’s audit lessons point to access control and BES cyber-system evaluation. [01-c1] [01-c5]

NERC’s computational-load standards point to site data, communications protocols and reliability operations. [01-c2] [01-c5]

MITRE’s update points to detection categories for prompt injection, AI-enabled exfiltration, AI result poisoning and attacks on AI-assisted defenses. [01-c3] [01-c5]

Together, these developments suggest that AI is being governed as a controlled actor, a software feature, a detection problem and a grid load, rather than as a standalone abstract technology category. [01-c5]

## The limits of the evidence

The strongest evidence here is US-centric and heavily focused on electricity and adjacent infrastructure concerns. [01-c1] [01-c2] [01-c3]

FERC’s audit item concerns audited entities and CIP-networked environments, not a finding about the entire US power sector or critical infrastructure more broadly. [01-c1]

The term “super intelligence” is also broader than agentic AI, because the reported examples include chatbots, personal assistants and automated analytical systems. [01-c1]

NERC’s standards activity concerns AI data centers, crypto mining facilities and other computational loads, so it speaks to AI infrastructure as grid load rather than to autonomous AI agents controlling operations. [01-c2]

MITRE’s ATT&CK update shows that AI-assisted activity is entering threat-modeling frameworks, but it does not by itself establish frequency, operational impact or prevalence across sectors. [01-c3]

The remaining uncertainty is therefore material: the evidence shows governance absorption, not a complete picture of deployment, failure rates or operator readiness. [01-c5]

## What to watch

- Whether FERC and NERC move from general risk consideration to specific evidence expectations for AI tools touching CIP assets and BES Cyber Systems. [01-c1] [01-c5]

- Whether computational-load standards produce verifiable obligations for site data, communications protocols and operational mitigation between AI data centers and reliability authorities. [01-c2] [01-c5]

- Whether MITRE-style AI techniques become routine in OT detection engineering, exercises and audit evidence, rather than remaining threat-intelligence taxonomy. [01-c3] [01-c5]
